tagline: Lake Huron’s coastal road links lighthouses, bays and maritime history
intro: North of Standish, US 23 becomes a two-lane coastal drive, following Saginaw Bay and Lake Huron through woods and shore towns. The Sunrise Coast Pure Michigan Byway promotes its sandy beaches, lighthouses and trails along more than 200 miles of Lake Huron shoreline. The highway north of Standish received its scenic designation in 2004 as the Sunrise Side Coastal Highway.

US 23 began in 1926 with a more inland course between Standish and Mackinaw City. Around 1932, the state moved the Omer–Tawas City section onto the Saginaw Bay shore through Au Gres. Other relocations followed during the 1930s, and in 1940 the highway took its present lakeshore route between Rogers City and Cheboygan. The last gravel section, near Hammond Bay, was paved in late 1947 or early 1948, completing another stage of the road’s transformation.

Heading north from Standish, pass through Omer and Au Gres, then follow the bay toward Tawas City and East Tawas. The road follows Lake Huron to Oscoda, crosses the Au Sable River, and continues past Harrisville toward Thunder Bay and Alpena. Beyond Alpena, it curves past Long Lake and Grand Lake before returning to Lake Huron near Thompson’s Harbor State Park. US 23 bypasses downtown Rogers City, then follows the coast through Cheboygan to Mackinaw City.

moments.title: Tawas Point Light
moments.text: The first Tawas Point lighthouse lost its useful position because the land kept growing. Commissioned in 1853, it stood on a point that shifting sand extended by nearly a mile. Congress approved funding for a replacement in 1875, and the new lighthouse was completed in 1877. The second tower rises 70 feet including its base, with inner and outer brick walls separated by an air space. A Fourth Order Fresnel lens remains in place. The point was originally called Ottawa Point; its name changed officially in 1902. Tawas Bay, behind the point, offers shelter from storms, wind and waves coming from the north and northeast.

moments.title: Alpena and Thunder Bay
moments.text: Off Alpena, Thunder Bay’s protected shipwrecks range from nineteenth-century wooden paddle steamers to twentieth-century steel-hulled steamers. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration established the sanctuary in June 2000, making it the first national marine sanctuary on the Great Lakes. In 2014, its protected area expanded from 448 to 4,300 square miles. On the Thunder Bay River in Alpena, the Great Lakes Maritime Heritage Center presents exhibits on local wrecks and the lakes, alongside an archaeological conservation laboratory and education spaces. The sanctuary stretches east from the lakeshore to the international border.

moments.title: Old Presque Isle Light
moments.text: Old Presque Isle Light combines two-thirds stone with one-third brick. Built in 1840, its tower and dwelling deteriorated in harsh weather until Congress found a new station necessary in 1867. Congress had appropriated $5,000 for the original light two years before it was built. The Lighthouse Board chose a location about two miles north so vessels farther offshore could see the light. The new tower was designed to stand 113 feet tall, more than 80 feet above the old tower’s height. The old light is no longer operational and serves as a museum; both lighthouses stand on the peninsula east of Grand Lake.
